Dad's Care Information in One Place

His medication list, his doctors and the papers worth keeping together, with a date beside each and a list of what's missing.

Download PDF

Dad knows where everything is. The medication list is in his wallet, the doctor's card is on the fridge, and the letter from his last appointment is in the desk, probably the second drawer.

This page doesn't move any of it, and it doesn't ask you to understand it. It records where each thing is kept, how recent it is and who has it. Fill it in with Dad. They're his papers.

What to collectWhere it's keptIts dateWho has it
Medication list: prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins and supplements
His doctors, with phone numbers
His pharmacy
Recent letters or visit summaries from his doctor
Care instructions he's been given, if any
Therapies or services he already uses, and who provides them
Other records or test results he's been given
Emergency contacts
The family's own dated notes on how he manages

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

What's missing, and who will ask for it

Anything above with an empty line. Put a name next to each. None of it has a deadline.

For example The list in his wallet is dated two years ago. Dad will go over it with the pharmacist at his next refill.

How to use it

  • Write the date printed on each item. If it has no date, write “undated.”
  • Note where each thing came from: Dad, his doctor's office, the pharmacy.
  • Leave everything where Dad keeps it. This page is a map, not a new filing system.
  • No need to copy out what a document says. Where it is and its date are enough.
  • When something changes, such as a new medicine or a new doctor, update the line and its date.

What this page doesn't do

It records where Dad's papers are, not what they mean. If a letter or an instruction isn't clear, the person who wrote it is the one to ask.

Ready for the next step?

You know where Dad's care information is kept, how recent each piece is and what isn't there. The care interview puts it to use: it goes through his situation area by area, with this page beside you, and turns your answers into a Family Care Profile you can bring to any care conversation.

Where this comes from

The medication row follows the Family Caregiver Alliance's advice to keep one updated list of everything a person takes. The doctors and emergency-contact rows follow the CDC's list of what a family's care information should include. The rest come from the Family Care Roadmap's working list for this step.
